cards.back: One character speaks to a silent listener, revealing their mind through what they choose to say. TRF: Changez speaks; the American never gets a line.
Narration that speaks to 'you'. Changez calls the American 'you', which puts the reader in the American's chair for the whole novel.
A story inside a story. The present-tense Lahore café evening frames Changez's past-tense story of Princeton, Erica, 9/11 and Chile.
A narrator we can't fully trust. Changez admits he may misremember or exaggerate, and he alone controls what we learn.
Telling the past from after it happened. Changez narrates his New York years already knowing how they end.
The American reaches into his jacket; Changez sees a glint of metal and hopes it's a business-card holder. Hamid never says which.
A story where characters stand for bigger ideas: Changez and Erica as Pakistan and America; Underwood Samson as U.S. power.
We only infer his words from Changez's replies, so our own assumptions fill the gap. Who is threatening whom is the reader's problem.
One evening: afternoon (gates locked) to sunset (lights, blackout) to dusk (bats) to night (walk to the hotel). Tension rises as it darkens.
Hints of what's to come. The American's hand going to his jacket early on is echoed on the last page.
An object standing for an idea. 'Underwood Samson' abbreviates to U.S., standing for America itself.
A repeated image or idea that builds a theme. Nostalgia recurs: Erica for Chris, America for its pre-9/11 self.
A direct comparison without like/as. Erica describes turning grief into writing like an oyster making a pearl.
Comparison with like/as. In ch.3 the American is like an animal unsure whether it is predator or prey.
The opposite of what you'd expect. Changez is trained to 'focus on the fundamentals' of finance and ends up seen as a fundamentalist.
The reader suspects more than a character. We sense danger at the café long before anything is confirmed.
Wordplay on two meanings. 'Fundamentals' (valuation) vs 'fundamentalism' (religion).
A reference to a real event or text. The janissaries allude to Ottoman history; 9/11 roots the novel in real events.
Placing opposites side by side. Changez's limousine next to the jeepney in Manila; the shabby Lahore house vs Manhattan.
Repeating words at the start of clauses. Changez repeats 'This was...' when he sees his family home in ch.9.
Word choice and what it reveals. Changez's formal, courtly 'sir' marks him as polite but performing.
Tone = the writer's/narrator's attitude. Mood = the feeling created in the reader. Changez's polite tone creates a tense mood.
Sentence shape for effect. 'And then I smiled.' The short sentence lands like a confession.
Setting or weather mirroring feeling. Dusk falls and bats gather as Changez reaches 9/11 in his story.
Human qualities for non-human things. America is pictured as brought 'to her knees' on 9/11.
A soft word for a harsh thing. 'Downsizing' (ch.7) means mass layoffs.
Two contradictory words together. 'Reluctant fundamentalist': hesitation vs zealous certainty.
Ethos = credibility, pathos = emotion, logos = logic/evidence. The three classic persuasive appeals in non-literary texts.
Non-literary: ads, blogs, infographics, speeches, opinion columns, news articles, posters, cartoons, letters, websites, brochures.
Look at: image, slogan, logo, colour, layout, typography, call to action, target audience, and how they work together.
Look at: statistics, charts, icons, colour coding, layout and visual hierarchy, captions, sources.
Narrator: Pakistani Princeton graduate, top Underwood Samson trainee, now a university lecturer in Lahore telling his story to the American.
Silent listener at the Lahore café: keeps his jacket on, sits with his back to the wall, swaps cups. Threat or threatened? Never settled.
Changez's love interest, met in Greece; aspiring novelist who can't move past Chris. Often read as 'Am-Erica'.
Erica's childhood best friend and boyfriend who died of lung cancer. Stands for an idealised past she can't let go of.
Senior man at Underwood Samson who hires and mentors Changez; grew up 'dirt poor'. Later says Changez betrayed his trust.
Changez's closest trainee friend; father from Barbados; ranks second. Tells him to 'focus on the fundamentals' and warns him to shave.
Underwood Samson vice president who tells recruits the firm is a meritocracy that ranks them and cuts the weakest.
Head of the Valparaíso publishing firm. Tells the janissary story, which makes Changez walk away from the job.
Mother appraises Changez and later warns him Erica is fragile. Father, a businessman, talks down to him about Pakistan.
In Manila he glares at Changez's limousine; Changez feels closer to him than to his American colleagues.
Recurring café waiter the American fears. Changez says his hard face comes from the north-west mountains. Follows them at the end.
1 Lahore meeting, Princeton, Jim. 2 Greece, Erica, Chris. 3 Training, ranked first. 4 Erica's parents. 5 Manila, 9/11 smile, airport. 6 Post-9/11 NY.
7 New Jersey, 'fundamentals', Afghanistan. 8 Erica's relapse, slur. 9 Lahore, beard, clinic. 10 Valparaíso, janissaries. 11 Let go, Erica gone. 12 The ending.
On his last evening in Manila he watches the towers fall on TV and smiles: at the symbolism of America humbled, not at the deaths.
Flying back, he is stripped to his underwear in a secure room; his colleagues go on ahead and he reaches Manhattan alone.
Both: he abandons the Chile assignment in ch.10, then is formally let go and escorted out in ch.11.
She vanishes from the clinic; her clothes are found above the Hudson. Suicide is suggested, never stated. Her mother gives Changez the manuscript.
A Lahore university lecturer who urges students to disengage from the US and criticises Pakistan's US ties on TV.
The frame setting: a café in Old Anarkali market. Changez is host, the American the guest, which reverses the usual power.
Changez's university (class of 2001): the meritocracy's gateway. He hid his jobs from richer classmates.
He feels 'immediately a New Yorker' though never American. After 9/11 the city fills with flags and suspicion.
Philippines assignment valuing a music company; he acts American ('play-acting') and sees 9/11 on his hotel TV.
Chile, last assignment: valuing a publishing house. The janissary story and the ruins make him walk away.
Elite valuation firm whose initials spell U.S.: America's promise of merit and its creed 'focus on the fundamentals'.
Grown in Lahore, kept in New York: to Changez a protest and symbol of identity; to Americans, a sign of threat.
Christian boys taken by the Ottoman Empire and trained to fight their own people, 'ferocious and utterly loyal'. Changez sees himself in them.
Fundamentals of finance vs religious fundamentalism. 'Reluctant' questions what the reader assumes.
Flags everywhere in New York: patriotism that shuts outsiders out, and nostalgia for an earlier America.
A simple story of a girl alone on an island, not the grief memoir Changez expected: Erica choosing her own path.
Frame details (ch.4-5) that make the American flinch: they build menace and foreshadow the ending.
Identity & belonging, East vs West, American Dream, power & privilege, 9/11 & aftermath, appearance vs reality, prejudice, nationalism.
Erica retreats into memories of Chris; Changez sees post-9/11 America in the same 'dangerous nostalgia' for its past.
Princeton → hired on the spot → ranked first → first-class travel → 9/11 → beard → walks out in Chile → let go.
Erica's father's condescending remarks and the rich classmates' treatment of Changez as exotic: polite prejudice before the attacks.
Airport strip search, rumours of attacks on Muslims, a slur in a parking lot, stares at the beard.
Hamid's 2013 newspaper essay, paired with the novel: readers wrongly project religious fundamentalism onto Changez.
Topic sentence (choice + named theme), Context (1-2 lines), Evidence (short quote/paraphrase), Analysis, Evaluation (how effective), Link to theme.
Writer + Verb + Technique + Purpose + Idea. E.g. 'Hamid uses juxtaposition to highlight how 9/11 transforms Changez's identity.'
'Hamid effectively uses ___ to depict the theme(s) of ___.' One dominant argument, not a device list. Avoid the verb 'show'.
Hook, title, author, 2007, dramatic monologue, brief context, key terms of the question defined, thesis. No plot summary.
Choice + theme, short context, the moment, analysis, effect on the reader, authorial intent, link back to the theme.
Restate the thesis in the question's words, synthesise (don't just summarise), authorial intent, and relevance of the text today.
Guided textual analysis of an unseen non-literary text (SL: one text, 1h15, 35%). Analyse the writer's choices and their effects.
Comparative essay on two literary works studied in class, answering one of four general questions (1h45, 35% at SL).
15 min: 10 min talk + 5 min questions. A global issue explored in one literary and one non-literary extract (30% at SL).
Ongoing record of your reading, annotations and responses. Not marked directly, but it's where IO ideas and evidence come from.

quiz.q: The Reluctant Fundamentalist is best described as a…
quiz.explain: One speaker (Changez) talks to a silent listener (the American) for the whole novel.

quiz.q: Why does the American never speak directly?
choices: Hamid forgot to give him lines
The monologue form means only Changez's voice exists
quiz.explain: Dramatic monologue: we only infer his words from Changez's replies, so we can't verify anything.

quiz.q: Changez's use of 'you' mainly…
choices: Places the reader in the American's seat
quiz.explain: Second-person address makes the reader the listener, so our own assumptions are tested.

quiz.q: The café evening in Lahore that encloses the New York story is called the…
quiz.explain: The present-tense frame surrounds the embedded past-tense story.

quiz.q: Changez is called an unreliable narrator mainly because…
choices: He controls and curates what we hear and admits he may exaggerate
quiz.explain: His unreliability is about control and self-interest, not obvious lies.

quiz.q: How does the novel end?
choices: Unresolved: a glint of metal as the American reaches into his jacket
quiz.explain: Hamid leaves it ambiguous; Changez hopes it's a business-card holder.

quiz.q: In which chapter does Changez watch 9/11 on TV?
quiz.explain: On his last evening in Manila, he sees the towers fall on TV and smiles.

quiz.q: What does Changez say his smile at 9/11 was really about?
choices: The symbolism of America being humbled
quiz.explain: He stresses it was the symbolism, not the victims, which still shocks the American.

quiz.q: Who hires Changez at Underwood Samson?
quiz.explain: Jim interviews him at Princeton and offers him the job on the spot.

quiz.q: Where does Changez first meet Erica?
quiz.explain: On the post-graduation Greece trip organised by rich classmates.

quiz.q: How did Chris die?
quiz.explain: Chris died of lung cancer; Erica never gets over him.

quiz.q: What story does Juan-Bautista tell Changez in Valparaíso?
choices: The story of Pablo Neruda's exile
The fall of the Twin Towers
quiz.explain: Christian boys taken by the Ottomans to fight their own people: Changez sees himself.

quiz.q: How does Changez's time at Underwood Samson end?
choices: He abandons the Chile job, then is let go
He moves to the London office
quiz.explain: Ch.10 he stops working in Valparaíso; ch.11 he is dismissed and escorted out.

quiz.q: What happens to Erica?
choices: She disappears from the clinic; her clothes are found by the Hudson
quiz.explain: Her fate is never confirmed; suicide is suggested, not stated.

quiz.q: Who tells Changez to 'focus on the fundamentals'?
quiz.explain: Wainwright says it during the New Jersey job in ch.7: the line behind the title's pun.

quiz.q: What does Changez become back in Lahore?
quiz.explain: He teaches and urges students to disengage from the US.

quiz.q: What do the initials of Underwood Samson spell?
quiz.explain: U.S. The firm stands for America and its economic power.

quiz.q: To Changez, the beard is mainly…
choices: A symbol of identity and protest
quiz.explain: He keeps it despite stares; to Americans it reads as a threat.

quiz.q: Erica is often read as a symbol of…
quiz.explain: 'Am-Erica': her nostalgia and retreat mirror post-9/11 America.

quiz.q: The title's 'fundamentalist' first refers to…
quiz.explain: Changez is first a fundamentalist of finance; the religious reading is the reader's assumption.

quiz.q: The janissaries are…
choices: Muslim boys trained to fight Christians
Christian boys taken by the Ottomans to fight their own people
quiz.explain: Muslim-for-Christian is a common mix-up. They were Christian boys turned into Ottoman fighters.

quiz.q: What fills New York after 9/11 that makes Changez feel shut out?
quiz.explain: The flags show patriotism turning inward and aggressive.

quiz.q: Which theme fits Changez 'play-acting' as an American in Manila?
quiz.explain: He performs Americanness for status, and the jeepney driver's glare exposes it.

quiz.q: Erica's father lecturing Changez about Pakistan shows…
quiz.explain: Polite condescension happens before the attacks; 9/11 just makes it louder.

quiz.q: Which pairing shows the nostalgia parallel?
choices: Erica's longing for Chris and America's longing for its past
quiz.explain: Both retreat from the present into an idealised past.

quiz.q: 'Pretend I am him' (Changez to Erica) best develops…
quiz.explain: To be loved he has to become Chris, which mirrors how he erases himself to fit in America.

quiz.q: 'Downsizing' for mass layoffs is an example of…
quiz.explain: A soft word for a harsh reality, typical corporate language.

quiz.q: 'Reluctant fundamentalist' is an example of…
quiz.explain: Two clashing words: hesitation and zealous certainty.

quiz.q: The bats and darkening evening mirroring rising tension is…
quiz.explain: Setting reflects mood; the café darkens as the menace grows.

quiz.q: Which is a NON-literary text for Paper 1?
quiz.explain: Paper 1 uses non-literary texts: ads, blogs, infographics, speeches, articles…

quiz.q: An ad's line 'Buy now and save!' uses…
choices: A call to action with imperatives
quiz.explain: Command verbs tell the audience exactly what to do.

quiz.q: Quoting a doctor in a health blog mainly appeals to…
quiz.explain: An expert borrows credibility (ethos).

quiz.q: In TCEAEL, what does the second 'E' stand for?
quiz.explain: Topic, Context, Evidence, Analysis, Evaluation, Link. Evaluation = how effective the choice is.

quiz.q: Which is the best thesis?
choices: Hamid uses many devices like metaphor, simile and irony.
This essay will show the theme of identity.
The novel is about a man in Lahore.
Hamid uses symbolism and the dramatic monologue to depict how identity is decided by others after 9/11.
quiz.explain: One clear argument: choices + named theme + what Hamid reveals. Not a device list; avoid 'show'.

quiz.q: What should NOT go in the introduction?
quiz.explain: Intro = hook, title, author, date, brief context, key terms, thesis. No quotes or plot retelling.

quiz.q: The 'magic sentence' formula is…
quiz.explain: E.g. 'Hamid uses the beard's symbolism to highlight how identity becomes visible after 9/11.'

quiz.q: The Individual Oral explores…
choices: A global issue through one literary and one non-literary extract
quiz.explain: 10 min talk + 5 min questions, built around a global issue.

quiz.q: Paper 2 at SL is…
choices: A comparative essay on two literary works studied
quiz.explain: 1h45, 35%: compare two works you studied in class in answer to a general question.

quiz.q: What is the Learner Portfolio?
choices: Your ongoing record of reading and responses
quiz.explain: It's not marked directly but it feeds your IO and essays.
